lailai.name: Lailai Xiaolong
lailai.glance: A small, busy soup-dumpling shop on a side street behind Nanjing Road East, popular with locals and visitors for crab xiaolongbao at everyday prices.
history: Xiaolongbao, 'little basket buns', come from Nanxiang, a town north-west of Shanghai, where they were first sold in the 19th century. Shanghai’s version has a thin, pleated skin around pork filling and hot broth made from gelled pork stock that melts when steamed.
lailai.meaning: Autumn is crab season in Shanghai, and crab-roe xiaolongbao (蟹粉小笼) are the seasonal treat: richer and more expensive than plain pork. Eat them the local way: lift one gently into the spoon, bite a small hole, sip the soup, then dip in black vinegar with ginger.

highlights.name: Crab xiaolongbao
highlights.what: The house favourite in reviews: thin skin, rich buttery broth.

highlights.name: Fried pork chop
highlights.what: Crisp and not greasy, several reviewers say.

highlights.name: Shrimp and crab wonton soup
highlights.what: A good extra if you are hungry.

tips: Queues are common around meal times; late morning is easier.
Order and pay at the counter or by scanning the QR code with Alipay; Mastercard may not be accepted.
Let the dumplings cool for a minute: the soup is very hot.
Lailai has more than one outlet (there is also a Jing’an branch). This stop is the original one at 506 Tianjin Road, behind Nanjing Road East.

verdict.line: Worth it: proper Shanghai soup dumplings, cheap, a short walk from the hotel.

lailai.best: Late morning, before the lunch rush.

teamuseum.name: China National Tea Museum
teamuseum.glance: China’s national museum of tea, set among tea terraces below Longjing village: free, indoor, and the best rainy-afternoon companion to the tea hills.
history: Opened in 1991 in Shuangfeng village on the road up to Longjing, the museum tells the story of tea in China from wild leaves and imperial tribute tea to modern tea science. It sits among working tea gardens, so you see the bushes and the halls in one visit.
teamuseum.meaning: Tea is one of China’s great contributions to the world, and Hangzhou’s Longjing (Dragon Well) is its most famous green tea. The museum explains the six tea families (green, white, yellow, oolong, black and dark), how each is made, and the culture around it, from tea houses to the tea ceremony.

highlights.name: Tea History Hall
highlights.what: From the earliest tea records to the Tang dynasty ‘Classic of Tea’ by Lu Yu.

highlights.name: Tea Essence Hall
highlights.what: Over 300 kinds of tea, including compressed bricks and cakes.

highlights.name: Tea Ware Hall
highlights.what: Teapots and cups from the Neolithic to the Qing dynasty, including Yixing clay pots.

highlights.name: Tea Customs Hall
highlights.what: How different regions and peoples drink tea, with reconstructed scenes.

highlights.name: Tea room
highlights.what: Taste and buy tea at posted prices: the low-risk place to buy real Longjing.

tips: Free entry; bring your passport. Weekends may need a free reservation in the museum’s WeChat/Alipay mini-program (中国茶叶博物馆), released a few days ahead.
Sources disagree on the closing day (Monday or Tuesday); Saturday is open.
The halls are spread over a hillside garden: umbrellas help in the rain, but most of the visit is indoors.

verdict.line: Worth it, especially on a rainy afternoon after Lingyin and the tea village.

teamuseum.best: Afternoon after Longjing village; good in rain.

xiaohepark.name: Xiaohe Park
xiaohepark.glance: A former Sinopec oil depot on the Grand Canal, turned into a free public park by the Japanese architect Kengo Kuma. Its old oil tanks are pierced with over a thousand holes and glow like giant lanterns after dark. It is about 1 km west of Xiaohe Street, on Xiaohe Branch Road (小河支路).
history: The Xiaohe Oil Depot (小河油库) was built here in the 1950s as Zhejiang’s first modern oil store, supplied by boat along the Grand Canal. At its peak in the 1980s it handled about 560,000 tonnes a year. It closed in June 2019.

Instead of clearing the site, Hangzhou kept four old warehouses and seven oil tanks and asked Kengo Kuma & Associates to turn it into a park. It opened in stages from 2022, with a light, leaf-patterned canopy over terraces and sunken gardens, and exhibition space in the old red-brick warehouses.
xiaohepark.meaning: Xiaohe Park is one of China’s best-known examples of turning industrial land into public space, the same idea as London’s Tate Modern or Duisburg’s Landschaftspark. For locals it is a favourite evening walk and photo spot; for the canal it shows the newest layer of a waterway that has been working for 1,400 years.

highlights.name: Oil-tank lanterns (油罐灯笼)
highlights.what: The perforated tanks are lit from inside at night: the main photo.

highlights.name: The canopy and sunken garden
highlights.what: Kengo Kuma’s web-like canopy over the terraces and a round sunken garden.

highlights.name: Old warehouses
highlights.what: Red-brick depot buildings now used for exhibitions and cafés.

highlights.name: Canal wharf
highlights.what: The old loading wharf on the Grand Canal, where three rivers meet.

tips: Go after dusk (about 17:30 onwards) for the lit tanks. If the lights are off, it is still a pleasant canal walk.
Combine it with Xiaohe Street: about 1 km apart, 10–15 min on foot along the Xiaohe river (the close-up map shows the walking path).
Didi about 15 min from the EBO Hotel (5 km). Tell the driver 小河公园.

verdict.line: Unusual and very photogenic at night; 30–45 min with Xiaohe Street next door.

xiaohepark.best: After dark, when the tanks are lit

shops.name: Super Brand Mall
shops.walk: Next to the Oriental Pearl Tower, 5–10 min from the Shanghai Tower; Lujiazui station (Line 2) is next door
shops.buy: A big Lujiazui mall at 168 Lujiazui West Road (陆家嘴西路168号): fashion, Chinese and international brands, electronics, a supermarket for snacks to take home, and many restaurants, some with river views on the upper floors. Good for a rainy hour or dinner on the Pudong side.
shops.watch: Busy at weekends. Restaurants with a river view fill up around sunset; get a queue number early.

shops.name: Xiaomi Home flagship, Joy City
shops.zh: 小米之家 上海静安大悦城旗舰店
shops.walk: Metro Line 8 one stop north from People’s Square to Qufu Road, or Didi 10 min; same road as your hotel (Xizang Road), 2 km north
shops.buy: Xiaomi’s full Chinese range in one place: phones, the Xiaomi ecosystem (smart home, robot vacuums, scooters, kitchen gadgets, power banks), many products not sold in Singapore. Address: 166 Xizang North Road, Joy City South Tower 1F (西藏北路166号大悦城南座一层).
shops.watch: Listed as Xiaomi’s Shanghai flagship in 2019; check on Amap that it is still open before going. Chinese-market products may have Chinese-only software and Chinese plugs.

shops.name: Xujiahui tech block: Bainaohui and TPY Center
shops.zh: 徐家汇 百脑汇（中金国际广场）· TPY中心
shops.walk: Didi 10 min from Wukang Road, or Line 11 one stop from Jiaotong University to Xujiahui; from there Line 11 runs straight to Jiangsu Road for the poster centre
shops.buy: What’s left of Shanghai’s famous computer-market district. Bainaohui still has floors of IT and gadget stalls (PCs, parts, phones, accessories, gaming), mixed with esports and food. Next door, TPY Center (the rebuilt Pacific Digital Plaza, reopened 2024) is pitched as a tech showroom mall.
shops.watch: Much smaller than it used to be: Xujiahui’s big electronics bazaars closed as shopping moved online. Shenzhen’s Huaqiangbei is the real thing; this is the closest in Shanghai. Compare prices with JD.com before buying.
sources: The Paper: Who killed the computer market? (2024)

shops.name: Xiaomi Home, Hubin in77
shops.walk: 5–10 min from your hotel, in the in77 malls along Yan’an Road by the lake
shops.buy: Xiaomi phones, smart-home gear and gadgets, a short walk from the hotel: easy to drop in on any evening in Hangzhou.
shops.watch: Map listings show it in in77 C or E zone; check the zone in Amap. Not confirmed as a flagship.

shops.name: Wensan Road digital street
shops.zh: 文三路数码街（颐高数码 · 西溪数码港）
shops.walk: Didi 15–20 min from Xixi on the way back to the lake
shops.buy: Hangzhou’s electronics street: several digital malls in a row (Yigao Digital Plaza, Xixi Digital Port and others) with stalls for PCs, parts, phones, cameras and accessories. Hangzhou’s old Electronics Market on Dengyun Road (登云路639号) is the place for components.
shops.watch: Our sources are from 2017; some malls may have shrunk or closed. Check Amap before going, and treat it as a look-around rather than a big shopping stop.
